ledger.settled: Locator-contract injection: a generic shared component defines a typed identifier config (e.g. GridLocators: root, header_cells, rows, cell_template) declaring WHAT it needs; app-specific Layer 2 owns the VALUES (page class constants or per-app locator module); FIXTURES wire values into the component at construction (conftest rule 3 stays absolute — no intra-L2 construction). Shared components are ordinary fixture-built L2 objects injected into Layer 3 side-by-side with page objects. Same-instance assertions preserved via the component's own fixture. Contract v2.3 narrows L2 rule 1 accordingly (identifier config / composed L2 components may be injected, never constructed internally). Honest limit stated: locator contracts fit structurally similar widgets; alien widgets get their own app-specific component — the generic set is an offered toolkit, not a forced abstraction.
ledger.notes: Dry-tested against QNXT claims-search grid (TC-001 flow) + platform-selenium employees table — one class, two apps, zero component changes. First version (page constructs its own components) REJECTED after user challenge: it required amending conftest rule 3; the fixture-injection model needs only the narrower rule-1 wording fix. Grid chosen as dry-test subject deliberately (worst case: most identifiers, v2's documented duplication failure zone, heaviest real workload).

ledger.settled: Variants without subclassing: when variants differ only in IDENTIFIERS → one generic class + per-variant config (v2's three dashboard subclasses become one DashboardComponent + three DashboardLocators). When variants differ in BEHAVIOR → app-specific component COMPOSES the generic one (has-a, never is-a: ApprovalGrid receives a GridComponent via its fixture and delegates). All nine v2 component files map onto config-variants or has-a with nothing left over. Exemplar strategy: MODAL leads the _reference set (simplest complete demonstration of the pattern); GRID is the flagship/stress example (dry-tested, most copied in practice).
ledger.notes: v2's dashboard_component_superclass + my_work_grid_superclass cited as the inheritance anti-pattern this replaces (architecture reference only, clean-room). Composition wiring happens in fixtures, consistent with the locator-problem settle.

ledger.settled: Definition: a shared component is a Layer 2 class encoding the MECHANICS of a recurring UI pattern, whose identifiers are injected rather than owned, subject to every Layer 2 rule, shipping in _reference/components/. Membership test (stated in the doc for the generating agent): usable by a different client's app unchanged, given only an identifier config → shared; otherwise app-specific. The line is economic as well as structural: shared components are platform IP (ship once, reuse per client); app-specific L2 is client deliverable. Maintenance triggers differ: shared components change when a UI pattern evolves; app-specific L2 changes when the client's app changes.
ledger.notes: DRY-TESTED against all nine v2 files + QNXT cases: clean sort, HOLDS with two sharpenings folded into the definition: (1) the test classifies CLASSES not PATTERNS — a failing class may contain an extractable shared pattern (v2 org_hierarchy fails as written but yields a TreeComponent that passes); FAIL has two exits: leave app-specific, or extract mechanics then re-test. (2) 'Generic' may be LIBRARY-generic, not universal — a date-picker is generic across apps sharing a widget library only; shared components declare scope (universal vs library:<name>). File-upload constraint noted: input-element path only, native OS dialogs not browser-automatable. platform-selenium has no components at all — rebuild-per-client cost only shows at enterprise scale.

ledger.settled: DEFERRED — consciously, per the 'contract-touching decisions early, catalogs on demand' rule. Trigger to revisit: Phase 4 harness design OR first client onboarding, whichever comes first. v1 ships only the two exemplars (modal, grid). Candidates on record for when the trigger fires: navbar, wizard, file-upload (README sketch) + date-picker, type-ahead (gap-check candidates) + tree (extractable from v2 org-hierarchy per the class-vs-pattern exit). The set self-assembles: the agent builds new components on demand per the settled pattern + membership test.
ledger.notes: User challenge ('why are we even doing this — shouldn't this be settled when the time arises?') drove the deferral. The speculative half of the section was inventory-picking; the load-bearing half (classifier, injection pattern, contract wording) was already settled.

ledger.settled: Shared components are ordinary fixture-built Layer 2 objects delivered to Layer 3 side-by-side with page objects. NO intra-L2 construction anywhere — conftest rule 3 stays absolute. App-specific L2 owns identifier VALUES (page class constants or per-app locator module); fixtures read them and wire generic components. Behavior wrappers (e.g. ApprovalGrid) receive their composed generic component via fixture injection. Same-instance assertions preserved through the component's own fixture.
ledger.notes: Settled during the section-3/4 dry test via user challenge — the first model (page constructs its own components) was REJECTED because it required amending conftest rule 3; fixture injection needed only the narrower v2.3 rule-1 wording.

ledger.settled: _reference/components/ ships TWO exemplars in v1: modal_component.py (lead — the simplest complete demonstration of locator-contract injection + fixture wiring) and grid_component.py (flagship — pattern at full stress, dry-tested against QNXT claims grid + platform-selenium employees table). Each shared component declares its genericity scope (universal vs library:<name>). Further components are built on demand by the generating agent from the pattern + membership test — the exemplars ARE the teaching material, not a catalog.
ledger.notes: Exemplar/stress-test distinction from user challenge ('why such a complex grid as reference?'): teaching exemplar wants simplest-complete (modal); dry test wants worst case (grid). Both ship, serving different jobs.
